title: Wide-column stores with Cassandra
goal: By the end, you can read a Cassandra table as sorted groups of rows on disk, say what an insert, an update and a delete each leave behind, explain why a table of deleted rows can make reads fail, and pick the right tool for a question the table wasn't built for.
opening:
At the end of each day, the payments app pays every shop what it took. A small program, the payout worker, keeps the waiting payouts in a small table, one row each. It reads the next ten, pays them and deletes their rows.

On the first morning, that read is instant. By evening it has slowed down, and the database's log is full of warnings. On the fourth day, the read fails.

It's easy to think that a delete makes a table smaller, the way deleting a row shortens a spreadsheet. Every delete here comes back at once, so nothing looks wrong.

DynamoDB single-table design and transactions kept an account's items together under one key, sorted. Cassandra, a free database program that spreads its data over many computers, builds its whole model on that shape. In this lesson, we'll read a Cassandra table as sorted groups of rows, watch what a write leaves on disk, and fill a group with deletes until reads fail. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payout worker keeps one shop's waiting payouts as rows in Cassandra, and deletes each row once the payout is paid. Today 50,000 payouts came and went for shop M-0042, and 10 are waiting. What does reading the next 10 cost?
options: About 10 rows: deleted rows are gone, so only 10 are left
About 50,010 entries: every delete left a marker that the read has to step over
Nothing extra after a few minutes, because Cassandra clears out deleted rows right away
It depends only on the limit, because Cassandra stops after 10 rows
warmup.why: In Cassandra, a delete writes a marker called a tombstone. The marker stays for 10 days by default, so that the other copies of the data can't bring the row back. A read from the start of the shop's rows steps over every marker before it finds 10 live rows. Past 100,000 markers in one read, Cassandra gives up on the read. The limit counts the rows you get back, not what Cassandra had to read to find them. The third section builds all of this up.

sections.h: A table is a map of partitions, each a sorted list of rows
sections.body:
Let's start with the question the payment history answers: account A-1001's 20 newest payments, out of 50 million. Cassandra runs on a cluster, a group of computers that work as one database, and each computer in it is called a node. You talk to it in CQL, the Cassandra Query Language, which looks like SQL. Model the access patterns first wrote down the six questions this app asks, called access patterns and numbered AP1 to AP6. It gave this one, AP1, its own table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE payments_by_account (
    account_id   text,
    created_at   timestamp,
    payment_id   text,
    merchant_id  text,
    status       text,
    amount_minor bigint,
    currency     text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, payment_id ASC);
```

Read the `PRIMARY KEY` line from the inside out. The inner parentheses hold the partition key, `account_id`. Every row with the same partition key belongs to one partition, so all of A-1001's payments form one group. The columns after it, `created_at` and `payment_id`, are clustering columns. They set the order of the rows inside the partition.

How does Cassandra find A-1001's partition among 50 million payments? The node that takes your request, called the coordinator, hashes the partition key. It runs a function that turns `'A-1001'` into a large whole number called a token, and always the same number for the same key. A-1001's is -4994511478997274402. Picture every possible token laid out around a circle, the ring from Why other data models exist, with each node in charge of some stretches of it. The token's place on the ring picks the nodes that keep copies of the partition, its replicas, usually three. Each replica holds the whole partition, so a query that names the partition key talks only to those nodes. The Partitioning track builds the ring properly.

Inside the partition, the rows are kept sorted by the clustering columns: newest `created_at` first, with `payment_id` breaking ties between payments in the same millisecond. That order is how they sit in memory and on disk. So "the 20 newest" means "the first 20 rows of one partition". A time window is one unbroken slice: the node jumps to the first row inside the window and reads until it leaves it. Oldest first is the same slice, read from the other end.

Picture a drawer of payment slips for each account, filed by date, newest at the front. The drawer is the partition, and the date order is the clustering columns. To find this morning's slips, you open one drawer and lift out one run of slips. The other 50 million payments stay where they are.

This shape gives the family its name, wide-column, and the name misleads. A partition can hold a great many rows, so it's a "wide" row of entries. It has nothing to do with a column store, which keeps each column's values together for reports.

A partition never splits across nodes, so its size is your decision. The Cassandra docs advise under 100,000 rows and under 100 MB. Do the sums before you pick the key: the rows in a partition are the write rate times how long the partition key stays the same. Keyed by shop alone, the table for the shop dashboard (AP3) grows forever. Add the day, `((merchant_id, day), ...)`, and a shop taking 40,000 payments a day fills a partition with 40,000 rows, about 6 MB at 150 bytes a row. On the busiest shopping day of the year, the biggest shop takes 5 payments a second, 432,000 a day, far past the row guideline. For that table, an hour bucket (18,000 rows) is the safer choice. The bucket costs reads: a week of history is 7 day partitions, or 168 hour partitions read in parallel and merged. Size it for your busiest key, not your average one.

The rules for queries follow from the picture. The partition key needs `=` on every one of its columns, or there's no token and no node to ask. Clustering columns can be limited only from the left, because that's the only order the rows are in, with at most one range at the end. A range of `created_at` is fine; a `payment_id` without a `created_at` is not. Anything else means reading rows and throwing most of them away. CQL refuses that unless you add `ALLOW FILTERING`, which the last section measures. So you build one table per question, and the app writes each payment to every table that needs it.

**Cassandra never edits a partition in place. Every write adds a new dated entry, and every read merges them.** The stepper shows the sorted list. The next two sections add the dated entries, starting with what one write leaves behind.

sections.h: Every write adds and nothing is edited: commit log, memtable, SSTable
sections.body:
A payment changes state several times. It's AUTHORIZED when the customer's bank sets the money aside, CAPTURED when the money really moves, and SETTLED when the shop has been paid. Say the app records each change as an `UPDATE` of the `status` column. What does that leave on disk?

In PostgreSQL, the database of the SQL track, an `UPDATE` first finds the row. The part of the file that holds it must be in memory, which often means a read from disk before the write can happen. Cassandra, which Facebook first built to search its users' inbox messages, takes the other road. A write never reads anything first, and a file is never changed once it's written.

Here's the path every write takes on a node. The node adds the write to the end of its commit log, a file on disk that's only ever appended to, so the write survives a crash. It also puts the write into the memtable, a sorted table in memory. Then it answers "done". When the memtable fills up, the node flushes it: it writes the whole memtable to disk as an SSTable, a sorted file that never changes afterwards. Nothing is looked up first. This is the LSM design (log-structured merge) that Why other data models exist sketched. Three things follow from it, and each one surprises people who learned SQL first.

First, `INSERT` and `UPDATE` are the same operation, an upsert. An `UPDATE` of a row that doesn't exist creates it. An `INSERT` of a key that already exists overwrites the columns it names, with no error about a duplicate key. "Insert only if it's absent" needs a lightweight transaction, in the last section.

Second, every value in a row, called a cell, carries its own write timestamp, in microseconds. The Java driver 4.19, the library a Kotlin or Java program uses to talk to Cassandra, stamps each statement with the clock of the computer the app runs on. (Its default, `AtomicTimestampGenerator`, does this unless the statement says `USING TIMESTAMP`.) When a read finds two versions of a cell, the higher timestamp wins, column by column. That rule is called last write wins, and the Replication track's lesson on concurrent writes shows which writes it silently drops. An `UPDATE` of `status` writes only the status cell. So after two flushes, the row exists as two pieces in two SSTables, and every read stitches them together. The Try-it dumps both pieces.

In the drawer picture, nobody ever rubs out a slip. To change a payment, you file a newer slip for it with the time stamped on it, and a reader keeps the slip with the latest stamp. The picture breaks on the stamps. A clerk would notice two slips stamped a second apart by two different offices. Cassandra trusts whichever clock reads later, even a wrong one, so a computer whose clock runs 2 seconds fast wins arguments it shouldn't.

Third, a read may have to look in the memtable and in several SSTables. Two things keep that cheap. Each SSTable has a Bloom filter, a small summary that can answer "this partition is definitely not in this file", so the read skips files. And compaction keeps the number of files down. In the background, it merges several SSTables into one new file, keeps the newest version of each cell and drops the rest. Which files it merges, and when, is the compaction strategy. The default in the settings file of Cassandra 5.0.9 is size-tiered, which merges files of similar size. Time-window groups data by when it was written, which suits rows that all expire after the same time. Cassandra 5.0 added the Unified Compaction Strategy (UCS), which can be tuned to behave like the older ones. Its docs recommend it "for most workloads", so for a new table on 5.0, start with UCS.

Updates leave old pieces behind until compaction tidies them. Deletes leave something stranger. Next, we'll see what.

sections.h: Why a delete is a write too: tombstones, TTL and the tombstone storm
sections.body:
Let's delete a test payment, pay-81655, from A-1001's history. Its three replicas are on nodes A, B and C, and C is down for an hour. The first version of a delete removes the row from A and B. Then C comes back, and repair runs. Repair is how Cassandra brings the copies back into agreement. Replicas compare their data, during reads (read repair) and in a background job (anti-entropy repair), and copy over whatever one of them lacks. The Replication track's lesson on leaderless replication builds both. Here, repair finds a row on C that A and B don't have. Nothing tells it whether A and B lost the row or deleted it, so it copies the row back. The deleted payment returns.

So Cassandra makes a delete a write. It writes a tombstone, a marker with a timestamp that says "this row was deleted at this time". In the drawer picture, it's a red "void" slip, filed like any other. The tombstone takes the same path to every replica and beats older versions by the same timestamp rule. Now repair has something to spread, and C gets the tombstone too.

How long must a tombstone stay? Until every replica has it. Cassandra can't know when that is, so it keeps each tombstone for `gc_grace_seconds`, 864,000 seconds or 10 days by default, and only then lets compaction drop it. That gives the people who run the cluster a deadline: repair every node more often than every 10 days. Say a node stays down for longer, then rejoins and is repaired. It still has the old row, and the tombstone that should hide it is gone everywhere else. Repair copies the row back, and the delete is undone. People call those rows zombies.

A TTL, short for time to live, works the same way. `INSERT ... USING TTL 86400` gives the cells an expiry time 24 hours ahead. That suits idempotency keys, the one-time values that stop a request from running twice. After the TTL, the cells are dead. Reads skip them and count them as tombstones, and compaction drops them once `gc_grace_seconds` have passed.

Now the opening's failure. The payout worker uses a table as a queue, a list of jobs waiting to be done: one partition per shop, one row per payout, sorted by payout id. It deletes each row once the payout is paid. Every delete leaves a tombstone at the front of the partition, and the tombstones stay for 10 days. When the worker asks for the next 10 payouts, the read starts at the front and steps over every tombstone before it finds 10 live rows. After 1,990 paid payouts, it handles 2,000 entries to return 10. With more than 1,000 tombstones in one read, Cassandra logs a warning (`tombstone_warn_threshold`). With more than 100,000, it gives up on the read (`tombstone_failure_threshold`). That's a tombstone storm, and the Try-it starts one.

**A delete leaves a marker that reads step over for 10 days. Don't use a partition as a queue.**

There are two fixes. One: start the read after the tombstones. The worker keeps the last payout id it paid and asks for `payout_id > ?`, so the node jumps past the dead rows, as the figure shows. On the same partition with 1,200 tombstones, that read reports "Read 3 live rows and 0 tombstone cells". Two: don't delete at all. Put a time bucket in the partition key and let old buckets expire with a TTL, on the time-window compaction strategy, which drops whole expired files. A real work queue belongs in Kafka, a program that keeps a log of messages and lets other programs read it, where reading a message doesn't delete anything.

Every rule so far assumed you know the partition key. Next, we'll ask questions that don't.

sections.h: Questions the key can't answer: ALLOW FILTERING, SAI indexes and lightweight transactions
sections.body:
Sooner or later someone asks a question the tables weren't built for. Support wants every FAILED payment from today, from any account. The CQL error from Model the access patterns first offers `ALLOW FILTERING`, and it's tempting, because on a laptop it works. The Try-it's trace, a step-by-step report of what the node did, shows the cost. It says "Submitting range requests on 17 ranges", then "Executing seq scan across 1 sstables", then "Read 7 live rows". The node walked every slice of the ring and read every row of every partition to return two. With 50 million payments on 12 nodes, each such request reads 50 million rows on 12 nodes. `ALLOW FILTERING` is fine in one case: when the query also names the partition key, so the cost is one partition, which you've already kept small.

The second choice is a new table, `failed_payments_by_day`, written next to the others. For anything the app runs often, that's still the answer.

The third, new in Cassandra 5.0, is a storage-attached index, or SAI: `CREATE INDEX ... USING 'sai'`. Each node indexes only its own data, and the index files are built and merged along with the memtable and SSTables they describe. A query on `status` alone now reads only the matching rows. But it still asks every node, because any node may hold a FAILED payment: the trace still says 17 ranges. So SAI is right for a query that runs a few times a minute, or to filter inside one partition (`account_id = ? AND status = ?`). It's wrong for a request that customers wait on thousands of times a second, and every write pays to keep the index up to date.

The last tool fixes something the write path made impossible. AP4 says an idempotency key may be used once. Two retries of the same payment reach two coordinators at the same moment. Both `INSERT` the key, and both succeed, because an insert is an upsert. The later timestamp wins, and both requests believe they created the payment. `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS` turns the insert into a lightweight transaction, or LWT. First the replicas agree that the row is absent, using a round of Paxos, a method for several computers to agree on one value even when some of them fail. Only then do they write. The reply has an `[applied]` column, and when it says `False`, it carries the row that won.

The CQL docs warn that LWTs "incur a non-negligible performance cost", because a Paxos round adds several round trips between replicas. Use them for the few writes that must not race, like claiming a key. The Transactions track's lesson on transactions in NoSQL shows how Paxos makes this safe. It also shows what Accord, planned for Cassandra 6, adds for transactions across partitions.

This lesson treated the cluster as one box that stores partitions. The Partitioning track opens the box in two lessons. The first covers the inside of a Cassandra cluster: the token ring, how nodes learn about each other, and how a coordinator runs a read or a write. The second sets a cluster up and keeps it healthy with `nodetool`.

b.src:
UPDATE payments.payments_by_account SET status = 'CAPTURED' WHERE ...;

== nb-1-big-Data.db  (the original insert, unchanged)
'2026-11-07T09:00:00.000Z', 'pay-81723' | [amount_minor=2500 ts=1794081362991451], ...,
                                          [status=AUTHORIZED ts=1794081362991451]
== nb-2-big-Data.db  (the update: one cell)
'2026-11-07T09:00:00.000Z', 'pay-81723' | [status=CAPTURED ts=1794081383953194]

-- a read merges both pieces; compaction later writes one merged row

compare.note: PostgreSQL keeps one current version of each row, and an update has to find the row before it writes. (Old versions stay only until no reader needs them.) Cassandra never finds anything before a write. It adds the new cell with its timestamp, and the old one stays on disk until compaction merges the files. That's why Cassandra writes are cheap and steady under load, and why its reads may touch several files. It's also why a plain write never says "row not found" or "duplicate key", and why a delete has to be a marker instead of an erase.

worked.title: Redesign the payout queue so reads never wade through tombstones

steps.say: Write the access patterns first. The worker asks for one shop's oldest waiting payouts; support looks a payout up by its id. A busy shop has about 30,000 payouts a day.
steps.code:
P1  next waiting payouts of a merchant, oldest first   ~every second
P2  one payout by id                                    ~a few per minute
volume: 30,000 payouts a day for M-0042

steps.say: The first draft is a queue: one partition per shop, and a delete for each row once it's paid. Count what a read meets after one day. Tombstones live 10 days, so they pile up.
steps.code:
PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id), payout_id)       -- delete when paid

after 1 day:   ~30,000 tombstones at the front of M-0042's partition
after 4 days:  ~120,000 -> past tombstone_failure_threshold: P1 fails

steps.say: Stop deleting. Bucket by hour, so a partition only ever holds one hour of payouts, and record the state as a column. Let whole buckets expire after a week (604,800 seconds) with a TTL, on the time-window compaction strategy, which drops expired files whole.
steps.code:
CREATE TABLE payouts_by_merchant_hour (
    merchant_id  text,
    hour         timestamp,
    payout_id    timeuuid,
    status       text,
    amount_minor bigint,
    PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id, hour), payout_id)
) WITH default_time_to_live = 604800
  AND compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy',
                    'compaction_window_unit': 'DAYS', 'compaction_window_size': 1};

steps.say: The worker keeps its place: the hour bucket and the last payout it handled. Each read starts after that point, so it never reads old rows at all. Marking a payout paid is an update of one cell, not a delete. (A `timeuuid` is an id that also records when it was made, so payout ids sort in time order.)
P2, the lookup by id, gets its own small table, written with the payout. It expires with the same TTL, so nothing is ever deleted by hand.

lab.title: Build one Cassandra table: sorted partitions, SSTables, tombstones and compaction
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder with the command above. They need no Docker: the lab is a small Kotlin model of a Cassandra table. All twelve fail with `NotImplementedError`, Kotlin's way of saying a function's body is still a `TODO`.

Read `WideColumnTable.kt`. `insert`, `delete`, `flush` and `repairFrom` are given. Writes only ever add a `Version` to the memtable, and `flush` turns the memtable into an `SSTable` that never changes. Each `Version` is a whole row with one timestamp; real Cassandra keeps one per cell.
Write `filteringReason`, following rules 1 to 5 in its KDoc comment (the documentation above the function). The messages are Cassandra's own, from the Try-it in Model the access patterns first.

Write `mergedPartition`: for each clustering key, the newest version across the SSTables and the memtable. Then write `select`: refuse a query that breaks the rules, pick the partitions, walk the merged rows, count live rows and tombstones, and stop at the limit. Ten tests pass now, the tombstone storm among them.

Write `compact`. The last test is the zombie from the tombstone section, made real: drop a tombstone after `gc_grace`, repair from a replica that missed the delete, and the row comes back. Change `gcGrace` in the test to 60 and watch the first half of that test fail, then put it back.
hints: Rule 1 is one line: `if (!q.where.keys.containsAll(key.partitionKey)) return ALLOW_FILTERING`.
For rule 3, the limited columns are `q.where.keys + listOfNotNull(q.range?.column)`. A clustering column at index `i >= fixed` that's limited is a gap, unless `i == fixed` and it's the range.

In `mergedPartition`, the sources are `sstables.mapNotNull { it.partitions[partition] } + listOfNotNull(memtable[partition])`. Use `newer(version, old)` to decide, never `>` on timestamps yourself: it handles a tie, where the tombstone wins.
In `select`, skip rows outside the slice with the given `inSlice` only when `filteringReason(q)` is null. A filtering query reads every row of the partition, and that cost is what the test checks.
In `compact`, `v.deadSince(now)` is null for a live row. Drop a row when `deadSince + gcGraceSeconds <= now`.

drill.title: Claim a key once, and follow a delete to the end
drill.prompt: From memory, write the CQL table for AP4 (an idempotency key and the payment it created), the statement that claims a key exactly once and expires after 24 hours, and what the reply looks like when the key is taken. Then list, in order, what happens to a row from `DELETE` until it's gone from disk.

answer.src:
CREATE TABLE payments.idempotency_keys (
    idem_key   text PRIMARY KEY,
    payment_id text
);

INSERT INTO payments.idempotency_keys (idem_key, payment_id)
VALUES ('idem-7f3a', 'pay-81723')
IF NOT EXISTS USING TTL 86400;

--  [applied] | idem_key  | payment_id      when the key is taken:
--      False | idem-7f3a |  pay-81723      the reply carries the winner

-- a DELETE, from start to end:
-- 1. a tombstone with the delete's timestamp goes to the commit log and memtable of each replica
-- 2. reads see it shadow every older version of the row, and count it as a tombstone
-- 3. flushes and compactions carry it along for gc_grace_seconds (864000 s, 10 days)
-- 4. repair spreads it to any replica that missed it, inside those 10 days
-- 5. after that, the next compaction of its files drops the tombstone and the row together

recap: A Cassandra table is a map of partitions. The partition key is hashed to a token that picks the replicas, and inside a partition the rows are sorted by the clustering columns, so a time window is one slice. A partition never splits: keep it under 100,000 rows and 100 MB, where rows = write rate × bucket length.

Writes never edit in place. Each one goes to the commit log and the memtable, and later into an SSTable that never changes. `INSERT` and `UPDATE` are both upserts, every cell carries a write timestamp (the app's clock, with the Java driver), and a read merges the pieces it finds: the newest timestamp wins.
Compaction merges SSTables and drops old versions. UCS, new in 5.0, is the strategy its docs recommend for most workloads.
A delete or an expired TTL is a tombstone, kept for `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days) so repair can spread it. Repair more often than that, or deleted rows come back as zombies.

Inserting and then deleting rows in one partition causes a tombstone storm: a warning past 1,000 tombstones in a read, a failed read past 100,000. Keep queues in Kafka, use time buckets with TTLs, and start reads after the dead rows.

The limit: off the key, every tool costs. `ALLOW FILTERING` reads every partition (fine only inside one), an SAI index still asks every node, and `IF NOT EXISTS` adds a Paxos round, so keep it for the few writes that must not race.
closing:
We started with a payout worker whose read of ten rows got slower every day. Each delete had added a tombstone that the next read had to step over, and every tombstone stays for 10 days.

Open the photos or notes app on your phone and delete something. Many apps don't erase it. They move it to a "Recently deleted" folder and keep it for about 30 days before it's really gone. A tombstone is a deleted mark with a timer too, kept for a different reason: so every copy hears about the delete.

Next, we'll meet MongoDB, a database that stores each record as a whole tree of fields, and ask what can safely live inside one record.

quiz.q: Table `payments_by_account` has `PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id)`, with `created_at` stored newest first. Which query reads one unbroken slice of one partition?
options: `WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' AND created_at >= '2026-11-07' AND created_at < '2026-11-08'`
`WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-07' ALLOW FILTERING`
`WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' AND payment_id = 'pay-81723'`
`WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' ORDER BY amount_minor DESC`
quiz.why: It gives the partition key with `=` and one range on the first clustering column, so the node jumps to the window and reads until it leaves it. Without the account, there's no token. `payment_id` alone skips `created_at`, which leaves a gap that Cassandra refuses without `ALLOW FILTERING`. And `ORDER BY` works only on clustering columns, in the stored order or its reverse.

quiz.q: Two parts of the app set the status of pay-81723 one second apart, first to CAPTURED and then to VOIDED, both with plain `UPDATE`s through the Java driver. The computer that sends the second update has a clock running 3 seconds slow. What does a read return afterwards?
options: VOIDED: Cassandra applies writes in the order they arrive
An error, because two updates touched the same cell
CAPTURED: each cell keeps the highest timestamp, and the driver stamped the second update with the slow clock
Both values, for the app to choose between
quiz.why: The Java driver 4.x stamps each statement with the clock of the computer that sends it. The VOIDED write carries a timestamp 2 seconds older than CAPTURED's, so last write wins keeps CAPTURED on every replica, and the void disappears without an error. Cassandra never hands back two versions to choose between; that's what Dynamo, from Why other data models exist, does.

quiz.q: Why does Cassandra write a tombstone for a delete, instead of removing the row from each replica?
options: Because removing data from an SSTable would mean rewriting the whole file
So that a replica that missed the delete can't have the row copied back to the others by repair
So that the delete can be undone within `gc_grace_seconds`
Because tombstones make reads faster than missing rows
quiz.why: If the replicas that saw the delete forgot the row, repair would find it on the replica that was down and spread it back. The tombstone is newer than the row, so it wins the merge, and repair spreads the delete instead. It's true that SSTables never change, but the next compaction could still drop a deleted row. The copies on other nodes are the reason, as the Cassandra docs say. Tombstones can't be undone, and they make reads slower, not faster.

quiz.q: Support wants every FAILED payment of the day, a few times an hour, and the team adds `CREATE INDEX ... ON payments_by_account (status) USING 'sai'`. What does a query on `status` alone do now?
options: Reads one partition, because the index stores the partition of every FAILED payment in one place
Asks every node, and each node reads only its matching rows through its own index
The same full scan as `ALLOW FILTERING`, because SAI only works with a partition key
It's refused: an indexed column still needs `ALLOW FILTERING`
quiz.why: SAI is a local index: each node indexes its own SSTables and memtable. A query without a partition key can't know which nodes hold FAILED payments, so it visits every slice of the ring (17 in the Try-it). But each node reads only the matching rows instead of all of them. That's fine a few times an hour and wrong for a request customers wait on, where a table built for the question wins.

quiz.q: From Model the access patterns first: a Cassandra table for the shop dashboard (AP3) is keyed `((merchant_id), status, created_at, payment_id)`, with no day in the partition key. The busiest shop takes 5 payments a second. What goes wrong?
options: Cassandra refuses inserts once a partition reaches 100,000 rows
Queries for one status become scans, because status is a clustering column
Nothing: Cassandra splits a large partition across nodes when it grows
The shop's partition gains about 432,000 rows a day and never stops growing, far past the 100,000-row and 100 MB guideline
quiz.why: A partition never splits, so everything under one partition key stays on the same replicas and grows with the write rate: 5 a second is 432,000 rows a day. Nothing enforces the guideline, so nothing stops the writes. Reads, compaction and repair of that partition keep getting slower instead. Putting status first is what makes AP3 one slice. Add a time bucket to the partition key, sized for the busiest shop.

flashcards.front: What do the partition key and the clustering columns each decide?
flashcards.back: The partition key is hashed to a token, which picks the replicas and the partition. The clustering columns decide the sorted order of rows inside the partition.

flashcards.front: What happens on a Cassandra write, in order?
flashcards.back: Append to the commit log, add to the memtable, answer "done". Later the memtable is flushed to an SSTable that never changes. Nothing is read first.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between INSERT and UPDATE in Cassandra?
flashcards.back: Almost none: both are upserts that write cells with a timestamp. There's no duplicate-key error and no "row not found".

flashcards.front: Who sets a cell's write timestamp when you use the Java driver 4.x?
flashcards.back: The app: the default `AtomicTimestampGenerator` uses the clock of the computer the app runs on, unless the statement says `USING TIMESTAMP`.
How long compaction must keep a tombstone before it may drop it: 864,000 seconds, 10 days. Repair every node more often than that.

flashcards.front: At how many tombstones in one read does Cassandra 5.0.9 warn, and fail?
flashcards.back: It logs a warning past 1,000 (`tombstone_warn_threshold`) and gives up on the read past 100,000 (`tombstone_failure_threshold`).

flashcards.front: How big should a Cassandra partition be, and how do you keep it there?
flashcards.back: Under 100,000 rows and 100 MB, say the Cassandra docs. Rows = write rate × bucket length, so add a time bucket to the partition key, sized for the busiest key.

terms.plain: All the rows with the same partition key, stored together and sorted by the clustering columns, on each of the key's replicas.
The primary-key columns after the partition key. They set the order of the rows inside a partition.
A node's sorted table of recent writes, kept in memory and written to disk as an SSTable when it's full.
A sorted file of rows on disk that never changes once written. Compaction merges several into one.
A write that adds the row if it's absent and overwrites the named columns if it's there. Every Cassandra INSERT and UPDATE is one.
A dated marker that says a row or a cell was deleted or has expired. It's kept for gc_grace_seconds so repair can spread it.
Cassandra 5.0's index for columns outside the key. Each node indexes its own data, next to its memtable and SSTables.
A write with a condition (`IF NOT EXISTS`, `IF col = ?`) that the replicas agree on with a Paxos round before it's applied.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "Deletes in Cassandra are free, they come back in a millisecond. Let's keep the waiting payouts in a table and delete each one when it's paid." Explain what a delete really writes, why it has to, and what this design does to the worker's reads after a few days.
explain_back.answer: A delete in Cassandra doesn't remove anything. It writes a tombstone, a marker with a timestamp, along the normal write path, which is why it's fast. It has to be a write because the data lives on three replicas. If the replicas that saw the delete forgot the row, repair would find it on a replica that was down and copy it back. The tombstone is newer than the row, so it wins the merge, and repair spreads the delete instead. Cassandra keeps tombstones for gc_grace_seconds, 10 days by default, before compaction may drop them. In a queue partition, every paid payout leaves a tombstone at the front, and the worker's "next 10" read starts at the front, so it steps over all of them. At 30,000 payouts a day, the read meets 30,000 tombstones after one day. It logs warnings past 1,000 and fails outright past 100,000, after about four days. I'd keep the queue in Kafka, or bucket the table by hour with a TTL and have the worker read from its last position, so no read ever starts among the dead rows.

deeper.body:
Cassandra 5.0 also ships newer storage formats that its default settings file, `cassandra.yaml`, leaves off. The `cassandra_latest.yaml` in the same 5.0.9 image turns them on: memtables built as tries (`TrieMemtable`, a tree that shares the common beginnings of keys), the BTI SSTable format (`sstable: selected_format: bti`, which replaces the old partition index and summary files) and UCS as the default compaction. The default file sets `storage_compatibility_mode: CASSANDRA_4`, so a cluster upgraded from 4.x keeps writing files that 4.x could read. That's why the Try-it's files are named `nb-...-big-...`. A new cluster can start from `cassandra_latest.yaml` instead.

There's a fourth compaction strategy besides size-tiered, time-window and UCS. Leveled compaction arranges files in levels so that a read touches fewer of them, at the price of rewriting data more often.

Two tools are worth keeping. `sstablepartitions`, new in 5.0, lists the largest partitions in an SSTable, which is how you find the account that broke the 100 MB guideline before it hurts. `sstablemetadata` prints, among other things, an estimate of the tombstones in each file that compaction could drop.

Materialized views were Cassandra's attempt to keep the extra "one table per question" tables up to date for you: you declare a view with a different primary key, and the server writes it. The Cassandra docs still mark them experimental, and most teams write the extra tables from the app, often in a logged batch. A logged batch promises that if any statement in it is applied, all of them eventually are, which is what you want when one payment goes to three tables. It isn't isolated, though: a reader can see one table updated before the other.

The database researchers Michael Stonebraker and Andy Pavlo, in a 2024 survey, describe the wide-column model as a document model with one level of nesting: a partition key, then a sorted list of rows that each have their own columns. MongoDB, in the next lesson, allows any depth.

ScyllaDB speaks CQL and runs the same data model on an engine written in C++, so this lesson's tables and queries work there unchanged. Since its 2025.1 release, it's source-available (you can read the code, under limits on how you use it) rather than open source.
